place: A one-room hunting hut in autumn; meat from yesterday's kill has hung unwrapped near the doorway overnight, warm and humid.
outcome: The meat has been sitting too long in warm, humid air and already smells slightly off, but a hungry player eats it anyway. It satisfies hunger in the moment with no immediate sign of harm. A few hours later cramps and vomiting set in as the bacteria that took hold overnight do their work, leaving the player weak and dehydrated for the rest of the day.

numbers: how many hours before meat this warm and humid turns
odds of illness from how spoiled the meat already was
hours until symptoms show
how severe the illness is, from how spoiled the meat was

latent: how spoiled the meat already was, only found by smell or taste
state_after: meat: eaten, gone
player: hunger satisfied at first, then sick and weak a few hours later
stress: spoilage as a hidden property judged by smell and touch, not a countdown the player can see
temptation: hardcode 'meat spoils after N hours' and 'eating spoiled meat = illness' as a rule about meat specifically

place: A dry, open campsite in summer; strips of venison hang on a rack in full sun to dry into jerky.
lines: cut it thin and dry it over a few days
outcome: Thin strips in steady sun and dry air lose moisture over several days and become safe, long-keeping jerky. Partway through, an unexpected rain soaks the half-dried strips and undoes much of the drying. Left damp afterward instead of being re-hung and finished, the strips grow mould instead of curing, ruining the batch nobody meant to ruin.

numbers: how many days of sun are needed to dry meat cut this thin
how much of the drying so far the rain undoes
how many more damp hours before mould takes hold

latent: whether rain comes before the drying finishes, not known until it does
state_after: venison strips: ruined by mould, inedible
drying rack: holds mouldy strips instead of jerky
stress: a multi-day process that can be interrupted partway and land in a worse outcome than either finishing or never starting
temptation: write a rule specifically for 'venison drying in rain' instead of general wetness undoing dryness and enabling mould on anything organic

place: A cold shoreline hut at the start of winter; the player has just landed a good catch of fish and needs it to last the season.
lines: pack it in salt for winter
outcome: Gutting removes the organs that would rot fastest, salting draws out the remaining moisture, and packing the salted fish in a cold barrel keeps it edible for weeks. One fish in the catch was gutted carelessly, though, with a scrap of gut left inside; under the salt it rots anyway, invisible from outside the barrel until it is opened weeks later and the smell gives it away among otherwise good fish.

numbers: how much longer gutted fish keeps than ungutted
how much salt per fish is needed to preserve it
how many weeks salted fish keeps in cold storage

latent: whether every fish was gutted cleanly before salting, not checked until the barrel is opened weeks later
state_after: fish: salted and stored, one fish among them rotten under the salt from a missed scrap of gut
stress: a preservation process whose success is only checkable much later, and can fail silently on one item among many that succeeded
temptation: special-case 'fish plus salt equals preserved' without modeling that a poorly gutted fish rots under the salt anyway

place: A small smokehouse hut with poor ventilation, built for curing meat over a smouldering fire.
lines: build a smoky fire and hang the meat
I'll tend it myself all day
outcome: Damp, green wood smoulders instead of burning clean, throwing off heavy smoke that cures the hanging meat well over the day. The same smoke fills the poorly vented hut where the player stays to tend it, and by evening the meat is beautifully cured while the player is nauseous and headachy from hours of breathing the fumes in an enclosed space, a cost nobody set out to pay.

because: damp wood smoulders instead of burning clean
numbers: how much smoke a smouldering damp fire makes over a day
how many hours of smoke cures meat this size
how long before smoke this thick in an enclosed space sickens a person

state_after: meat: smoked, cured, keeps for weeks
player: nauseous, headache, needs fresh air
stress: a process that is good for one thing in the scene and harmful to a person nearby, from the very same cause
temptation: hardcode smoking a smokehouse as simply safe, instead of letting the same smoke that cures meat also harm anyone breathing it in an enclosed space

place: A damp stone cellar under a farmhouse, storing a loaf of bread nobody has touched in days.
outcome: With nobody touching it, the loaf sits in damp cellar air for days until mould visibly covers it. Rats that have been slipping into the cellar unseen find and eat the mouldy bread anyway, driven by hunger rather than caution. A day or two later one of the rats sickens and dies from the mould's toxins, a small death nobody was watching for that only shows up after the fact.

numbers: how many days of damp air before mould becomes visible
odds a hungry rat eats mouldy food anyway
how much mould toxin it takes to kill a rat, over how many days

latent: that rats have been visiting the cellar at all, unnoticed until the bread is gone or a dead rat turns up
state_after: bread: gone, eaten
cellar: a dead rat found in the corner, days later
stress: a chain that starts and ends with nobody watching, only explainable after the fact from what is left behind
temptation: special-case 'bread in a damp cellar goes mouldy' instead of general dampness plus time acting on anything organic, and mould as generally toxic to whatever eats it

place: A mixed forest floor after rain; a cluster of unfamiliar mushrooms has come up near the path.
lines: they look fine, just eat some
outcome: The player eats unidentified mushrooms without checking them, and this particular kind gives no warning taste or smell. Nothing seems wrong at first. Several hours later severe stomach pain and vomiting begin, and the deeper harm, to organs that quietly absorbed the toxin, does not show itself until a day or two after that, well past when the first symptoms seemed to be the whole story.

numbers: odds this species is the poisonous look-alike, given how common it is here
hours until the first symptoms show
days until the deeper harm shows

latent: whether this particular mushroom was the poisonous look-alike, not knowable by looking
state_after: player: fine-feeling at first, then badly ill hours later, and still recovering days after that
stress: a poison with no immediate warning sign and harm that outlasts the symptoms that first announce it
temptation: hardcode a specific mushroom species and a fixed damage number instead of a general poisonous property with a delayed, graded effect

place: A hillside pasture where a family keeps a milking goat; a patch of bitter, dark-leaved weed grows unchecked at the fence line.
outcome: The goat grazes the weed in among the grass with nobody watching, and it sickens over the following day. Nobody connects the goat's dull mood to the fence line, so it gets milked as usual, and the toxin passes into the milk. The family drinks it that evening and falls ill themselves hours later, a second, delayed harm from a plant none of them ever touched.

numbers: odds a grazing animal eats the poisonous weed among the grass

because: poisonous weed is toxic to livestock
numbers: hours until the goat visibly shows illness

because: family did not know goat was sick
effects: transfers toxin from goat to milk
numbers: how much of the toxin passes into the milk
hours until the milk-drinkers fall ill after the goat did

latent: that the goat grazed on the weed at all, unseen at the fence line
state_after: goat: sick, off its feed
milk: tainted, already drunk by the family
family: ill, with no obvious cause to them
stress: a poison that travels from plant to animal to person along an ordinary chain nobody set up on purpose
temptation: special-case 'this weed poisons goats' without letting the toxin also transfer through milk to whoever drinks it

place: A dry trail in summer heat; a shrinking, still pond, green-tinged, is the only water for miles.
lines: just drink it, I'm so thirsty
outcome: Desperate for water, the player drinks from the stagnant pond, and it quenches thirst at once. Hours later cramping and diarrhea set in from whatever the still water was carrying, and the fluid lost to sickness leaves the player thirstier and weaker than before drinking at all, the fix having deepened the problem it was meant to solve.

numbers: odds standing water this still carries something harmful
hours until symptoms begin
how much fluid is lost to the sickness afterward

state_after: player: thirst gone for a while, then sick and more dehydrated by evening
stress: a fix that solves the immediate need while making the underlying problem it was meant to solve worse
temptation: hardcode 'pond water equals bad' as a flag instead of a general still-versus-moving property that applies to any water source

place: A larder shelf; a clay jar of crushed berries and honey, sealed tight, set aside to ferment weeks ago.
outcome: Fermentation keeps working inside the sealed jar with nobody tending it, and the gas it gives off has nowhere to go. Over several days pressure builds until it cracks the seal and the jar bursts on its own, spraying fermented mess across the larder. The strong smell draws a stray scavenging animal in from outside, an unintended visitor nobody invited over a jar nobody was even watching.

numbers: how many days of fermenting before pressure becomes a problem
how much gas pressure the sealed jar can hold before it fails
how far the smell draws a scavenger from

latent: how far along the fermentation had gotten, unknown until the jar is opened or bursts on its own
state_after: clay jar: broken, contents lost
larder: sticky mess and animal tracks
stress: a slow process that keeps running unattended until it forces itself on someone's attention
temptation: special-case 'sealed jar of fermenting fruit explodes' instead of general gas buildup inside any sealed container of something fermenting

place: A hunting trail, third day without a catch; the player's boots and leather belt are the only leather at hand.
lines: chew on the leather, better than nothing
outcome: Leather is not food: the player can chew and swallow strips of the belt, but there is nothing in it the body can draw nourishment from, so real hunger returns almost as fast as before. The tough, undigested strips sit heavy, giving cramps and a bloated feeling for a while, and a poorly chewed piece going down risks catching in the throat, all for no real gain.

numbers: how long the false fullness lasts before hunger returns
odds a poorly chewed piece catches in the throat going down
how soon real hunger returns after the false fullness fades

state_after: player: hungry again within the hour, uncomfortable, belt gone
leather belt: gone, chewed and swallowed
stress: an action that satisfies the verb 'eat' without satisfying the need behind it, because the thing has no food in it
temptation: hardcode a whitelist of 'edible things' instead of a general nourishment property that leather simply lacks

place: Deep pine forest at midday; the player is splitting firewood alone when the axe glances off a knot and bites into a shin.
outcome: The axe leaves an open, steadily bleeding cut on the shin. Wrapping it tightly with a cloth strip, done one-handed and in a hurry, slows the bleeding enough to walk, but the wrap is loose at the edges. Within an hour of walking on it the wrap works itself free and the bleeding starts again, needing a proper rewrap and rest to actually hold.

because: player's leg was in the path
numbers: how deep the cut is
how fast it bleeds
how well a rushed one-handed wrap holds compared to a careful one
how much movement it takes to work a loose wrap free

state_after: player: shin wound rebleeding after an hour of walking, needs a proper rewrap and rest
stress: a fix that works only as well as the care put into it, and can be undone by ordinary movement afterward
temptation: hardcode 'bandage equals wound fixed' instead of a bandage quality that depends on care taken and can come loose

place: A narrow gorge at dusk; the player's sword has been left resting in the campfire and pulled out coated in burning oil for a fight.
lines: light the sword and cut him
outcome: The blade is hot and briefly alight, and cutting flesh with it opens a wound while also burning the skin right at the edges. But the cut itself takes only a fraction of a second, far too brief for the heat to seal the blood vessels the way a held, steady cautery would. The wound still bleeds, now alongside a burn, and the attacker's clothing near the cut catches light too, a side effect nobody was aiming for.

because: sword was resting in the fire
numbers: how long the oil keeps burning on the blade
how deep the cut is
how much heat a blade passing this fast actually transfers

because: burning oil-coated sword touched it while alight
numbers: odds the brief contact is enough to catch cloth

sword: still alight, losing oil

place: A rocky scree slope; the player slipped and fell several feet onto uneven ground.
outcome: The fall snaps a bone in the lower leg. Splinting it with branches and cloth binds the leg roughly straight and stops the worst movement, but it does not set the bone properly. Swelling builds around the break over the following day regardless, and the leg needs real time immobilized and resting to knit, with a real risk of healing slightly crooked if walked on too soon.

because: branches and cloth is rigid enough to brace

place: A warm, cramped hut; the player's own cut on the forearm, three days old, was bandaged once and forgotten.
outcome: Nobody tends the wound for days, and under the bandage the edges turn red and swollen, warmth and puffiness setting in as an infection nobody watched for. Once noticed and treated with crushed herbs found nearby, the poultice eases the swelling and some of the pain, but it does not clear an infection already this advanced, and a fever follows a day later, needing more than herbs to fully turn back.

because: old wound stayed covered and damp
numbers: how many untended days before infection sets in
how much a poultice helps against infection this advanced
how many hours after treatment the fever still comes on

place: A festival night around the fire; a jug of last month's fermented berry wine gets passed around.
outcome: Cup after cup of the fermented wine leaves the player warm, loud, and increasingly clumsy, judgment loosening with each round, and stumbling near the fire becomes a real risk by the end of the night. The alcohol clears from the body over the following hours, but the next morning brings a pounding head and a raw stomach, the delayed price for the night before.

how many hours until sober
how bad the morning-after is, from how much was drunk

place: A high moor at night in early winter; the player fell asleep in the open without building a proper shelter or fire.
outcome: With nobody acting, the cold works on the sleeping player through the night. Shivering starts first, then fades as core temperature drops further, which is the dangerous part, since the shivering stopping can look like recovering when it is actually worse. Left long enough with nobody checking, this could kill; found and warmed in time, it costs a sick, sluggish day afterward instead.

place: An open scrubland trail at high summer noon; the player has been walking for hours with an empty waterskin.
outcome: Hours of heat and exertion with no water to replace what is sweated out bring on dizziness, an early warning that pushing on instead of resting in shade ignores. The player keeps going rather than stopping, and eventually collapses on the trail before reaching anywhere, a forced stop that costs far more time than resting earlier would have.

place: A hunting camp; a companion has a deep bleeding gash from a boar's tusk that a bandage alone can't stop.
lines: heat the knife and cauterize it
outcome: The knife is heated properly in the fire until glowing, then held steadily against the bleeding wound, unlike a passing cut. Because the contact is sustained rather than brief, this genuinely seals the smaller vessels and stops the worst of the bleeding, at the cost of a real burn injury layered onto the wound, and pain severe enough the companion needs holding down. The burn itself needs its own care afterward, or it risks turning septic in the following days.

numbers: how long in the fire until the blade is hot enough to cauterize

because: hot knife is held steady against the wound
numbers: how long the blade must stay in contact to seal the vessels

state_after: companion: bleeding stopped, but with a bad burn on top of the wound, in severe pain, needing the burn tended over the coming days
stress: a treatment that genuinely works, unlike the sword-cut version, because it trades sustained contact for a real, costly burn
temptation: hardcode 'hot metal to wound equals cauterized, no downside' instead of weighing contact time against the burn it also causes

place: A mountain pass; the player has been marching for two days and a night with barely any sleep to outrun bad weather.
lines: keep going, no time to stop
outcome: Pushing through without sleep, the player's judgment and coordination degrade the longer it goes on. Eventually a stumble on the uneven pass becomes a near-fall that a rested person would have caught easily, forcing the very stop that was being avoided and losing more time in the end than sleeping earlier would have cost.

temptation: hardcode 'no sleep for N hours equals stat penalty' instead of a compounding exhaustion state that creates its own accidents

place: A warm forest clearing where a deer, killed by a wolf and abandoned mid-meal, lies in the sun.
outcome: Nobody touches the carcass, but it does not stay still: warmth speeds the rot, flies arrive within the day, and by the second day the smell has drawn more wolves and a bear in from further off than the one that made the original kill, an unintended pull of danger into the clearing that started from an animal nobody was even watching.

how soon flies find a rotting carcass in the open
